source_refs.note: Exercise 14.3, Question 7 (i)-(iv): properties of the cross product from the definition (book p.283); (i) printed with a garbled symbol. Proofs, no key answer.

blocks.prompt: 7 (i) Use the definition of cross product, for any vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) and scalar \(k\), prove that \(\underline{u} \times (-\underline{u}) = \underline{0}\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof from the definition.
We must show the cross product of a vector with its negative is the zero vector.
Plan: find the angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(-\underline{u}\), put it in the definition.
steps:
Given: any vector \(\underline{u}\).
To prove: \(\underline{u} \times (-\underline{u}) = \underline{0}\).
Method: The definition (14.3.1)
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\]
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors and \(\hat{n}\) the unit vector given by the right hand rule.

The case \(\underline{u} = \underline{0}\)
\[\underline{0} \times \underline{0} = \underline{0}\]
Why: If either vector is zero, the length factor \(|\underline{u}| = 0\), so the product is \(\underline{0}\). From now on \(\underline{u} \ne \underline{0}\).

Angle between \(\underline{u}\) and \(-\underline{u}\)
\[\theta = \pi, \quad \sin\pi = 0\]
\[|-\underline{u}| = |\underline{u}|\]
Why: \(-\underline{u}\) has the same length as \(\underline{u}\) but points the opposite way, so the angle between them is \(180^{\circ}\).

Put it in the definition
\[\underline{u} \times (-\underline{u}) = |\underline{u}||-\underline{u}|\sin\pi\,\hat{n}\]
\[= |\underline{u}|^2(0)\,\hat{n} = \underline{0}\]
Why: The length of the product contains \(\sin\theta = 0\); a vector of length 0 is the zero vector.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In 7 (i) the book prints the left side with a garbled symbol, \(\underline{u} \times (-\_\,)\), and the right side as the number 0. The intended statement is \(\underline{u} \times (-\underline{u}) = \underline{0}\) (the zero vector).

blocks.prompt: 7 (ii) Use the definition of cross product, for any vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) and scalar \(k\), prove that \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof from the definition.
We must show that swapping the order changes only the sign.
Plan: compare the lengths, then the directions (right hand rule).
steps:
Given: any vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\) with angle \(\theta\).
To prove: \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -(\underline{v} \times \underline{u})\).
Method: Definition \[\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\]

Compare the lengths
\[|\underline{u} \times \underline{v}| = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\]
\[= |\underline{v}||\underline{u}|\sin\theta = |\underline{v} \times \underline{u}|\]
Why: The angle between the two vectors is the same \(\theta\) whichever comes first, and numbers commute.

Compare the directions
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{v}:\ \hat{n}, \qquad \underline{v} \times \underline{u}:\ -\hat{n}\]
Why: For \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) the fingers of the right hand curl from \(\underline{u}\) to \(\underline{v}\) and the thumb gives \(\hat{n}\); for \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) they curl the opposite way and the thumb points the opposite way.

Put length and direction together
\[\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = |\underline{v}||\underline{u}|\sin\theta\,(-\hat{n})\]
\[= -\left(|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\right)\]
\[= -(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: Same length, opposite direction. Multiplying both sides by \(-1\) gives \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -(\underline{v} \times \underline{u})\). (If either vector is \(\underline{0}\), both sides are \(\underline{0}\).)
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) (the cross product is anti-commutative)

blocks.prompt: 7 (iii) Use the definition of cross product, for any vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) and scalar \(k\), prove that \(\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v}) = (k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v} = k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).
blocks.explanation:
A proof from the definition, by cases on the sign of \(k\).
We must show a scalar can be taken out of either vector.
Plan: \(k > 0\), \(k = 0\), \(k < 0\) for \(\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v})\); then use part (ii) for \((k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v}\).
steps:
Given: vectors \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}\) with angle \(\theta\) and \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = |\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\); a scalar \(k\).
To prove: \(\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v}) = (k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v} = k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).
Method: Multiplying \(\underline{v}\) by \(k\) changes its length to \(|k||\underline{v}|\); if \(k < 0\) it also reverses it. We see what that does to the angle and to \(\hat{n}\).

Case \(k > 0\)
\[\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v}) = |\underline{u}|\,(k|\underline{v}|)\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\]
\[= k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: \(k\underline{v}\) points the same way as \(\underline{v}\), so the angle (\(\theta\)) and \(\hat{n}\) are unchanged; only the length becomes \(k|\underline{v}|\).

Case \(k = 0\)
\[\underline{u} \times (0\underline{v}) = \underline{u} \times \underline{0} = \underline{0}\]
\[0(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}) = \underline{0}\]
Why: Both sides are the zero vector.

Case \(k < 0\)
\[\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v}) = |\underline{u}|(-k)|\underline{v}|\sin(\pi - \theta)(-\hat{n})\]
\[= k\,|\underline{u}||\underline{v}|\sin\theta\,\hat{n}\]
\[= k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: \(k\underline{v}\) points opposite to \(\underline{v}\): its length is \(|k||\underline{v}| = -k|\underline{v}|\), the angle with \(\underline{u}\) becomes \(\pi - \theta\) and the right hand rule gives \(-\hat{n}\). Since \(\sin(\pi - \theta) = \sin\theta\) and \((-k)(-\hat{n}) = k\hat{n}\), we get \(k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).

Now \((k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v}\)
\[(k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v} = -\big(\underline{v} \times (k\underline{u})\big)\]
\[= -k(\underline{v} \times \underline{u})\]
\[= -k\big(-(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\big) = k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: Part (ii) swaps the order, the three cases above (true for any two vectors) take \(k\) out, and part (ii) swaps back.

Conclusion
\[\underline{u} \times (k\underline{v}) = (k\underline{u}) \times \underline{v} = k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
Why: Both products equal \(k(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\).

blocks.prompt: 7 (iv) Use the definition of cross product, for any vectors \(\underline{u}\), \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\) and scalar \(k\), prove that \(\underline{u} \times (\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = (\underline{u} \times \underline{v}) + (\underline{u} \times \underline{w})\).
blocks.explanation:
The distributive law, proved from the definition.
We must show \(\underline{u} \times\) distributes over a sum.
Plan: build \(\underline{u} \times \underline{x}\) from \(\underline{x}\) by three simple moves (project, turn, stretch); each move respects addition.
steps:
Given: any vectors \(\underline{u}, \underline{v}, \underline{w}\).
To prove: \(\underline{u} \times (\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = \underline{u} \times \underline{v} + \underline{u} \times \underline{w}\).
Method: If \(\underline{u} = \underline{0}\) both sides are \(\underline{0}\). Otherwise let \(\Pi\) be the plane through \(O\) perpendicular to \(\underline{u}\). We show that \(\underline{u} \times \underline{x}\) is obtained from any vector \(\underline{x}\) by three moves that each turn a sum into a sum.

Three moves that give \(\underline{u} \times \underline{x}\)
\[\underline{x} \to \underline{x}' \to \underline{x}'' \to |\underline{u}|\,\underline{x}''\]
Why: (1) \(\underline{x}'\) = projection of \(\underline{x}\) on \(\Pi\) (its "shadow" along \(\underline{u}\)); its length is \(|\underline{x}|\sin\theta\). (2) \(\underline{x}''\) = \(\underline{x}'\) turned through \(90^{\circ}\) in \(\Pi\), counter-clockwise when seen from the tip of \(\underline{u}\); it now points along \(\hat{n}\) of the right hand rule and still has length \(|\underline{x}|\sin\theta\). (3) Multiply by \(|\underline{u}|\). The result has length \(|\underline{u}||\underline{x}|\sin\theta\) and direction \(\hat{n}\), which is exactly \(\underline{u} \times \underline{x}\).

Each move turns a sum into a sum
\[(\underline{v} + \underline{w})' = \underline{v}' + \underline{w}'\]
\[(\underline{v}' + \underline{w}')'' = \underline{v}'' + \underline{w}''\]
\[|\underline{u}|(\underline{v}'' + \underline{w}'') = |\underline{u}|\underline{v}'' + |\underline{u}|\underline{w}''\]
Why: Projecting the triangle formed by \(\underline{v}\), \(\underline{w}\), \(\underline{v} + \underline{w}\) onto \(\Pi\) gives a triangle again, so the shadow of the sum is the sum of the shadows. Turning a whole triangle through \(90^{\circ}\) keeps it a triangle, so the turn of a sum is the sum of the turns. Multiplying by a number distributes over addition.

Put the moves together
\[\underline{u} \times (\underline{v} + \underline{w}) = |\underline{u}|(\underline{v} + \underline{w})''\]
\[= |\underline{u}|\underline{v}'' + |\underline{u}|\underline{w}''\]
\[= \underline{u} \times \underline{v} + \underline{u} \times \underline{w}\]
Why: Step 2 applied to \(\underline{v} + \underline{w}\), then step 3, then step 2 applied to \(\underline{v}\) and to \(\underline{w}\).

Check with an example
\[\underline{u} = \underline{i},\ \underline{v} = \underline{j},\ \underline{w} = \underline{k}\]
\[\underline{i} \times (\underline{j} + \underline{k}) = \underline{k} - \underline{j}\]
\[\underline{i} \times \underline{j} + \underline{i} \times \underline{k} = \underline{k} - \underline{j}\]
Why: Using \(\underline{i} \times \underline{j} = \underline{k}\), \(\underline{i} \times \underline{k} = -\underline{j}\) (and the determinant for the left side), both sides agree.
